title: Filtrations
objectives: Model information that grows over time with a filtration, and tell adapted from predictable.

screens.title: Information grows
screens.prose: Slide time from 0 to 3. At each time the tree shows only what you can tell apart: the visible ends are the atoms. Count them.
screens.question: Fill in the number of atoms at each time.

hints.text: Count the visible ends of the tree at each time.
Each new toss splits every end in two.
The counts go 1, 2, 4, 8, which is $2^n$.

feedback.correct: 1, 2, 4 and 8. Each toss doubles the atoms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to each time and count the visible ends.

byKey.r0c1: At time 0 nothing is seen, so every outcome is merged into one atom.
byKey.r3c1: At time 3 every toss is seen, so each of the 8 outcomes is its own atom.

explain.text: The atoms double with each toss: $1, 2, 4, 8$. Every atom at time $n$ splits into two at time $n + 1$, so nothing known is ever forgotten.

screens.title: Filtrations and adapted processes
screens.prose: The growing list $\mathcal{F}_0 \subset \mathcal{F}_1 \subset \mathcal{F}_2 \subset \mathcal{F}_3$ is a **filtration**. A process is **adapted** when $X_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable: at time $n$ it uses no future toss. Let $S_n$ be heads minus tails after $n$ tosses.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which processes are adapted?

options.text: $S_n$, the walk of heads minus tails
$\max_{k \le n} S_k$, the running maximum
$S_{n+1}$, the walk one step ahead of now
options.why: You used the next toss. At time $n$ only $n$ tosses are known.

options.text: $S_3$, the final value reported at time 1
options.why: You reported a final value early. At time 1 only one toss is known.

hints.text: Ask whether each value is decided by the first $n$ tosses.
The running maximum looks back, never forward.
Only $S_{n+1}$ and the early $S_3$ look ahead.

feedback.correct: The walk, its running maximum and $S_n^2 - n$ use only past tosses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reject any value that needs a toss after time $n$.

byKey.d: The value $S_{n+1}$ needs toss $n + 1$, which arrives after time $n$.
byKey.e: At time 1 you cannot know tosses 2 and 3, so $S_3$ is not yet decided.

explain.text: $S_n$, its running maximum and $S_n^2 - n$ are functions of the first $n$ tosses, so they are adapted. $S_{n+1}$ and an early $S_3$ need tosses not yet seen. Adapted means no peeking.

screens.title: A position is predictable
screens.prose: A position $H_n$ is held over step $n$, from time $n - 1$ to time $n$. It must be fixed at time $n - 1$, so $H_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable. Such a process is **predictable**.
screens.question: Which rule is predictable? Take $H_1 = 0$.

options.text: Hold 1 unit if toss $n - 1$ was H, else 0
Hold 1 unit if toss $n$ is H, else 0
options.why: You set the position from the move it earns. Toss $n$ is not known at time $n - 1$.

options.text: Hold 1 unit if $S_n > 0$, else 0
options.why: You used $S_n$, which includes toss $n$. The position must use $S_{n-1}$.

options.text: Hold $-1$ unit if toss $n$ is T, else 1
options.why: You flipped the sign after seeing toss $n$. That bets on a known result.

hints.text: At which time must the position be chosen?
Time $n - 1$, before toss $n$ is seen.
Only the rule built on toss $n - 1$ qualifies.

feedback.correct: The momentum rule uses toss $n - 1$ only, so it is known at time $n - 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reject any rule that uses toss $n$ itself.

byKey.b: You used toss $n$ to set the position for step $n$. That is look-ahead.
byKey.c: The sum $S_n$ ends with toss $n$, so it is not known when you must trade.

explain.text: The momentum rule reads toss $n - 1$, which is in $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$. The other rules read toss $n$, which is not. A predictable position can depend on the past, never on the move it earns.

screens.title: Which filtration
screens.prose: The natural filtration of a price $S$ is $\sigma(S_0, \dots, S_n)$. A trader who also sees the order flow works with a larger filtration. Both are filtrations on the same space.
screens.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The natural filtration is the smallest one to which $S$ is adapted
Every filtration to which $S$ is adapted equals the natural one
options.why: You read 'smallest' as 'only'. Add the order flow and $S$ is still adapted.

options.text: A signal built on order flow is adapted to the natural filtration
options.why: You assumed order flow is a function of the price. It can carry facts the prices have not shown.

options.text: The natural filtration grows when the trader sees more
options.why: You mixed up the two. The natural one is fixed by $S$, and extra information makes a different, larger one.

hints.text: What does the natural filtration contain?
Only what the price path has revealed.
Any filtration holding more still has $S$ adapted.

feedback.correct: It holds exactly what the price path reveals, so no filtration with $S$ adapted can be smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what each filtration contains.

byKey.b: Larger filtrations also make $S$ adapted, so there is no uniqueness.
byKey.c: Order flow can reveal more than the price, so it need not be adapted to the smaller filtration.

explain.text: $S_n$ is $\sigma(S_0, \dots, S_n)$-measurable by definition, so the natural filtration is the smallest with $S$ adapted. A bigger filtration keeps $S$ adapted and adds processes such as order-flow signals. Predictable now means predictable for the filtration you name.

screens.title: Gains on one path
screens.prose: The gains of position $H$ on the walk $S$ are $\sum_{k \le n} H_k (S_k - S_{k-1})$. Take the path H, H, T, H, with moves $+1, +1, -1, +1$. Momentum holds 1 unit after an H and starts at 0. Look-ahead holds $H_k = $ the sign of move $k$.
screens.question: Fill in the momentum positions and both gains.

hints.text: Momentum $H_k$ is 1 when toss $k - 1$ was H.
Tosses 1 and 2 were H and toss 3 was T, so $H = (0, 1, 1, 0)$.
Gain is $0(+1) + 1(+1) + 1(-1) + 0(+1)$. Look-ahead earns $|{\rm move}| = 1$ each step.

feedback.correct: Momentum is $(0, 1, 1, 0)$ with gain 0. Look-ahead gains 4, one for each step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each position by the move it earns, then add.

byKey.r3c1: At step 4 the previous toss was T, so momentum holds 0.
byKey.r4c1: Add $0 + 1 - 1 + 0$. The profit of step 2 is cancelled by the loss of step 3.
byKey.r5c1: Look-ahead holds the sign of each move, so it earns +1 on every one of the four steps.

explain.text: Momentum holds $(0, 1, 1, 0)$, so it gains $0 + 1 - 1 + 0 = 0$. Look-ahead holds $+1, +1, -1, +1$ and earns $1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$. The difference is that look-ahead sets $H_k$ from the move it earns.

screens.title: The look-ahead backtest
screens.prose: A backtest sets the position for step $n$ from the sign of move $n$: $H_n = X_n$. The coin is fair. A colleague says a fair game pays nothing, so the backtest should report 0.
screens.question: What expected gain does this backtest report over 10 tosses?

hints.text: What does the position earn on each step?
$H_n$ has the same sign as the move, so each step earns $+1$.
Add 10 steps of $+1$.

feedback.correct: 10, one per step. The rule trades a move it has already seen.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the gain of one step first.

byKey.zero: You applied the fair-game rule. It holds for predictable positions, and this one uses toss $n$ to trade toss $n$. That is a look-ahead backtest.
byKey.half: You counted only the steps that win. Look-ahead wins on every step, because it picks the winning side.
byKey.one: That is one step. The gain adds up over all 10.

explain.text: $H_n = X_n$ earns $X_n \times X_n = 1$ every step, so 10 over 10 tosses. Every predictable rule earns 0 on average, which is next lesson's theorem. The backtest is not wrong arithmetic, it is a position nobody could hold.

screens.title: Edge cases
screens.prose: Two small cases test the definitions. A deterministic process never changes with the coin. And $\mathcal{F}_0$ is trivial: at time 0 nothing has been tossed.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which statements are true?

options.text: A deterministic process is both adapted and predictable
$H_1$ must be a constant, because $\mathcal{F}_0$ is trivial
A predictable process is always adapted
Every adapted process is predictable, as it is known at time $n$
options.why: You reversed it. $S_n$ is adapted, but it depends on toss $n$, so it is not predictable.

hints.text: Test each claim on a deterministic process, then on $S_n$.
$H_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, and $\mathcal{F}_{n-1} \subset \mathcal{F}_n$.
Three are true. The reversed claim fails for $S_n$.

feedback.correct: Predictable implies adapted, a constant is both, and $H_1$ is constant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Predictable is the stronger property.

byKey.d: Adapted allows use of toss $n$. Predictable does not, so the converse fails.

explain.text: A constant is measurable for every sigma-algebra, so it is adapted and predictable. Because $\mathcal{F}_{n-1} \subset \mathcal{F}_n$, a predictable $H_n$ is adapted. The reverse fails for $S_n$.

screens.title: Gains and predictability in code
screens.prose: Write `gains(H, path)`, the gains of positions `H` on a path of tosses, and `is_predictable(strategy, n)`. Here `strategy(path, k)` returns $H_k$, and the check runs over all $2^n$ paths.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from itertools import product

def gains(H, path):
    """The gains sum_k H_k * (move k). H lists H_1..H_n; path is a string of H and T."""
    ...

def is_predictable(strategy, n):
    """True when strategy(path, k) depends only on path[:k-1], for k = 1..n."""
    ...
widget.prelude:
from itertools import product
momentum = lambda path, k: 1 if k > 1 and path[k - 2] == 'H' else 0
lookahead = lambda path, k: 1 if path[k - 1] == 'H' else -1
hold = lambda path, k: 1

tests.call: is_predictable(lambda path, k: 1 if k == 3 and path[2] == 'H' else 0, 4)

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. `momentum`, `lookahead` and `hold` are already defined, each as `rule(path, k)`. A rule is predictable when two paths that agree before toss $k$ give the same $H_k$.

hints.text: A move is $+1$ for H and $-1$ for T.
For predictability, group the paths by `path[:k-1]` for each $k$.
Within a group, `strategy(path, k)` must take one value.

feedback.correct: All 10 tests pass. Momentum gains 0 on the path, look-ahead gains 4, and only look-ahead fails the check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every $k$, not just the last.

explain.text: `gains` multiplies each position by its move. `is_predictable` groups paths by what is known before toss $k$ and demands one position per group. The look-ahead rule gives two positions inside a group, so it fails.

screens.title: Yesterday's close
screens.prose: A daily return is $+1\%$ or $-1\%$ with equal chance. A backtest sets day $n$'s position from the sign of day $n$'s own return. It earns $|r_n| = 1\%$ every day. A live strategy can only use yesterday's close.
screens.question: What does the backtest report over 250 days, in percentage points?

hints.text: What does the position earn on one day?
It always picks the winning side, so $+1\%$.
Multiply by 250 days.

feedback.correct: 250 points, from a position nobody could hold. A live rule averages 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one day's gain first.

byKey.zero: You gave the honest rule's average. This backtest uses today's close to trade today's return.
byKey.half: You counted half the days. A look-ahead position wins on every day.
byKey.one: You gave one day's gain. The backtest repeats it on all 250 days.

explain.text: The backtest wins $1\%$ on every day, so $250 \times 1\% = 250$ points, with no variation at all. That is why look-ahead bias inflates a Sharpe ratio without limit. Adapted is not enough for a position: it must be predictable.

ideas: A filtration is a growing list of sigma-algebras: information accumulates and is never lost. An adapted process uses no future toss.
A position held over step $n$ must be predictable: $H_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable. The gains are $\sum_{k \le n} H_k (S_k - S_{k-1})$.
Look-ahead sets $H_n$ from the move it earns. On a fair coin it gains 1 a step, though every predictable rule gains 0 on average.

formula.name: Adapted and predictable
formula.note: Further reading: Williams, chapter 10 (previsible processes); Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance I, chapter 2.

summary.trap: A signal built on today's close is adapted, not predictable. Using it to trade today's return is look-ahead.

quiz.prose: A trader holds 2 units on day $n$ if the price rose on day $n - 1$, and 0 otherwise.
quiz.question: Is this position predictable?

options.text: Yes: it uses only the previous day's move
No: it depends on the price, so it looks ahead
options.why: You thought any use of the price is look-ahead. Yesterday's price is known today.

options.text: No: it changes from day to day, so it is not fixed
options.why: You thought a changing position cannot be predictable. Predictable restricts the information, not the variation.

feedback.correct: Yesterday's move is known when the position is set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which day's move the rule reads.

explain.text: The rule reads the move of day $n - 1$, which is in $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$. So $H_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable.

quiz.prose: Take the path T, T, H, T, H with moves $-1, -1, +1, -1, +1$. A buy-the-dip rule holds 1 unit after a T and starts at 0.
quiz.question: What are its gains?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List $H_k$, then multiply by each move.

byKey.neg: You may have held after an H. The rule holds after a T.
byKey.three: You added the three steps where it held, without their signs. The first held step lost 1.
byKey.zero: You gave the average over all paths. The rule is predictable, so that average is 0, but this path gains 1.

explain.text: After T, T, H, T the positions are 0, 1, 1, 0 and 1. Multiplying by the moves gives $0, -1, +1, 0, +1$, which add to 1.

quiz.prose: At time 0 nothing has happened, so $\mathcal{F}_0 = \{\varnothing, \Omega\}$.
quiz.question: What can the first position $H_1$ depend on?

options.text: Only a constant
The first toss, as it is the first step
options.why: You used the move $H_1$ earns. It is not known at time 0.

options.text: Any past price, as for later steps
options.why: There is no past at time 0. Only constants are measurable for a trivial sigma-algebra.

feedback.correct: $H_1$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable, so it is a constant.

explain.text: A trivial sigma-algebra makes only constants measurable. So the opening position is fixed in advance.

quiz.prose: Let $M_n = \min(S_0, \dots, S_n)$ be the running minimum of the walk.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: $M_n$ is adapted, but not predictable
$M_n$ is predictable, since it only looks back
options.why: You noticed it looks back. It still includes $S_n$, the toss at time $n$, so it is not $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable.

options.text: $M_n$ is not adapted, since it uses all the history
options.why: You treated history as a problem. Adapted allows every toss up to time $n$.

feedback.correct: It uses the tosses up to time $n$, which is adapted but not predictable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the tosses used with $\mathcal{F}_n$ and $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$.

explain.text: $M_n$ is decided by tosses 1 to $n$, so it is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable. It changes when toss $n$ is a new low, so it is not $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable.
